title: Pod Basics: Deploy and Expose a Simple Application
objective: Create a Deployment that runs a single nginx pod and expose it via a Service of type ClusterIP.
context: A developer needs a quick local instance of a web server for testing static assets within the cluster.
tasks: Create a Deployment named `nginx-deploy` with the image `nginx:alpine` and 1 replica.
Expose the Deployment with a Service named `nginx-svc` on port 80.
Verify the Service endpoint resolves to the pod IP and returns the default nginx page.
Cleanup the resources.
hints: Use a Deployment manifest to manage pod replicas. See the Deployment docs: https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/controllers/deployment/
Expose a Deployment via a Service. Review Service types: https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/services-networking/service/#publishing-services-service-types
Validate the Service by curling the ClusterIP from another pod. Reference troubleshooting connectivity: https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/debug-application-networking/connect-applications-service/
solution:
cat <<'EOF' > kcna-001-deploy.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nginx-deploy
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nginx
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nginx
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nginx
        image: nginx:alpine
        ports:
        - containerPort: 80
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nginx-svc
spec:
  selector:
    app: nginx
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80
    targetPort: 80
EOF
kubectl apply -f kcna-001-deploy.yaml
validation_commands: kubectl run curl-pod --image=curlimages/curl --rm -i --restart=Never -- curl -s http://$(kubectl get svc nginx-svc -o jsonpath='{.spec.clusterIP}')
key_concepts: Deployments provide declarative updates and replica management.
Services expose a set of pods and give them a stable virtual IP.
ClusterIP is the default service type for internal cluster communication.
kubectl apply can create multiple resources from a single YAML file.

title: ConfigMap: Inject Configuration into Pods
objective: Create a ConfigMap with application configuration and mount it as a file inside a pod.
context: A micro‑service reads its configuration from a file at `/etc/config/app.conf`. You need to provide that file without baking it into the container image.
tasks: Create a ConfigMap named `app-config` from a local file `app.conf`.
Deploy a pod that mounts the ConfigMap at `/etc/config`.
Verify the pod can read the configuration file.
Cleanup the ConfigMap and pod.
hints: ConfigMaps store key‑value pairs or entire files. See the ConfigMap guide: https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/configuration/configmap/
Mount a ConfigMap as a volume to expose its data as files. Reference volume mounts: https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/storage/volumes/#configmap
Use `kubectl exec` to cat the file inside the running container.
solution:
echo 'greeting=Hello KCNA' > app.conf
kubectl create configmap app-config --from-file=app.conf
cat <<'EOF' > kcna-002-pod.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: configmap-pod
spec:
  containers:
  - name: busybox
    image: busybox
    command: ["sh", "-c", "sleep 3600"]
    volumeMounts:
    - name: config-volume
      mountPath: /etc/config
  volumes:
  - name: config-volume
    configMap:
      name: app-config
EOF
kubectl apply -f kcna-002-pod.yaml
cleanup: kubectl delete pod configmap-pod && kubectl delete configmap app-config && rm app.conf kcna-002-pod.yaml
key_concepts: ConfigMaps decouple configuration from container images.
A ConfigMap can be consumed as environment variables or as files via a volume.
Changes to a ConfigMap are reflected in pods that consume it (if mounted as a volume).

title: Secret: Store and Use Sensitive Data
objective: Create a Secret containing a password and consume it as an environment variable in a pod.
context: A small application needs a database password at runtime but you must avoid exposing the value in the container image or pod spec.
tasks: Create a Secret named `db-pass` with a key `password`.
Deploy a pod that reads the secret as an env var `DB_PASSWORD`.
Verify the pod can echo the password (without exposing it to the host shell).
Cleanup the Secret and pod.
hints: Secrets are base64‑encoded objects. See the Secret documentation: https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/configuration/secret/

Consume a Secret as an environment variable using `envFrom` or `valueFrom`. Reference env var injection: https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/inject-data-application/define-environment-variable-container/
Use `kubectl exec` to print the env var inside the container.
solution:
echo -n 's3cr3tP@ss' > password.txt
kubectl create secret generic db-pass --from-file=password=./password.txt
cat <<'EOF' > kcna-003-pod.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: secret-pod
spec:
  containers:
  - name: busybox
    image: busybox
    command: ["sh", "-c", "sleep 3600"]
    env:
    - name: DB_PASSWORD
      valueFrom:
        secretKeyRef:
          name: db-pass
          key: password
EOF
kubectl apply -f kcna-003-pod.yaml
validation_commands: kubectl get secret db-pass -o jsonpath='{.data.password}' | base64 -d
cleanup: kubectl delete pod secret-pod && kubectl delete secret db-pass && rm password.txt kcna-003-pod.yaml
key_concepts: Secrets keep sensitive data out of container images.
Kubernetes stores Secret data base64‑encoded; RBAC controls who can read them.
Environment variable injection is simple, but mounting as a file can be more secure for large data.

title: Service Types: Expose an Application Externally
objective: Expose a Deployment via a NodePort service and access it from the host machine.
context: A teammate needs to reach a demo web service running in the cluster from their laptop without using an Ingress controller.
tasks: Deploy a Deployment named `demo-app` running `httpd`.
Create a Service of type NodePort exposing port 80 on the cluster and mapping it to a host port.
Determine the allocated NodePort and curl the service from the host.
Cleanup the resources.
hints: NodePort services allocate a port in the 30000‑32767 range. See Service types: https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/services-networking/service/#type-nodeport
Use `kubectl get svc` to discover the assigned NodePort.
Access the service via `http://$(minikube ip):<nodePort>` from the host.
solution:
cat <<'EOF' > kcna-004-deploy.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: demo-app
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: demo
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: demo
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: httpd
        image: httpd:alpine
        ports:
        - containerPort: 80
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: demo-nodeport
spec:
  type: NodePort
  selector:
    app: demo
  ports:
  - port: 80
    targetPort: 80
    nodePort: 30080
EOF
kubectl apply -f kcna-004-deploy.yaml
key_concepts: NodePort exposes a service on each node's IP at a static port.
Useful for quick demos, but not recommended for production traffic.
Minikube forwards NodePort ports to the host automatically when started with `--ports`.

title: Ingress: Route HTTP Traffic with Host‑Based Rules
objective: Install an Ingress controller and configure an Ingress resource that routes traffic based on host name.
context: You need a single external endpoint that forwards requests to two different services (`app‑v1` and `app‑v2`) depending on the requested host.
tasks: Deploy two Deployments (`app-v1` and `app-v2`) each exposing port 80.
Create Services for each Deployment.
Create an Ingress that routes `v1.example.com` to `app‑v1` and `v2.example.com` to `app‑v2`.
Test the routing by adding host entries to /etc/hosts and curling each host.
Cleanup all resources.
hints: Ingress resources rely on an Ingress controller; minikube’s built‑in controller is enabled via the `ingress` addon. See Ingress docs: https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/services-networking/ingress/
Host‑based routing uses the `host` field in the Ingress rule. Review the rule syntax.
After creating the Ingress, the controller creates a LoadBalancer IP (often the minikube IP). Use `kubectl get ingress` to see the address.
solution:
cat <<'EOF' > kcna-005-manifests.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: app-v1
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: v1
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: v1
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: httpd
        image: httpd:alpine
        ports:
        - containerPort: 80
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: svc-v1
spec:
  selector:
    app: v1
  ports:
  - port: 80
    targetPort: 80
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: app-v2
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: v2
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: v2
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: httpd
        image: httpd:alpine
        ports:
        - containerPort: 80
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: svc-v2
spec:
  selector:
    app: v2
  ports:
  - port: 80
    targetPort: 80
---
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: demo-ingress
spec:
  rules:
  - host: v1.example.com
    http:
      paths:
      - path: /
        pathType: Prefix
        backend:
          service:
            name: svc-v1
            port:
              number: 80
  - host: v2.example.com
    http:
      paths:
      - path: /
        pathType: Prefix
        backend:
          service:
            name: svc-v2
            port:
              number: 80
EOF
kubectl apply -f kcna-005-manifests.yaml
validation_commands: echo '$(minikube ip) v1.example.com v2.example.com' | sudo tee -a /etc/hosts
cleanup: kubectl delete -f kcna-005-manifests.yaml && sudo sed -i '/v1.example.com/d' /etc/hosts && sudo sed -i '/v2.example.com/d' /etc/hosts
key_concepts: Ingress abstracts HTTP routing and works with a controller (NGINX, GCE, etc.).
Host‑based rules let a single IP serve multiple virtual hosts.
Minikube’s ingress addon provides a lightweight NGINX controller for local testing.

title: Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA): Scale Based on CPU Usage
objective: Create an HPA that automatically scales a Deployment from 1 to 3 replicas when CPU utilization exceeds 50%.
context: A web service experiences variable traffic. You need to ensure sufficient replicas during spikes without manual intervention.
tasks: Deploy a simple `php-apache` Deployment with resource requests for CPU.
Create an HPA targeting the Deployment with a CPU utilization threshold of 50% and a max of 3 replicas.
Generate load using `kubectl run busybox` to push CPU usage above the threshold.
Observe the replica count scaling up, then scale down after load stops.
Cleanup all resources.
hints: HPA requires the Metrics Server to provide CPU metrics. See metrics‑server docs: https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/metrics-server
Define CPU requests in the pod spec; the HPA works against the percentage of requested CPU.
Use `kubectl top pods` to view current CPU usage.
Load can be generated with `stress` or a busybox loop that curls the service repeatedly.
solution:
cat <<'EOF' > kcna-006-deploy.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: php-apache
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: php-apache
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: php-apache
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: php-apache
        image: php:8.2-apache
        ports:
        - containerPort: 80
        resources:
          requests:
            cpu: "200m"
---
apiVersion: autoscaling/v2
kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler
metadata:
  name: php-apache-hpa
spec:
  scaleTargetRef:
    apiVersion: apps/v1
    kind: Deployment
    name: php-apache
  minReplicas: 1
  maxReplicas: 3
  metrics:
  - type: Resource
    resource:
      name: cpu
      target:
        type: Utilization
        averageUtilization: 50
EOF
kubectl apply -f kcna-006-deploy.yaml
validation_commands: kubectl run load-generator --image=busybox --restart=Never -- /bin/sh -c 'while true; do wget -qO- http://php-apache; done'
sleep 60 && kubectl get hpa php-apache-hpa -o jsonpath='{.status.currentReplicas}'
key_concepts: HPA automatically adjusts replica count based on observed metrics.
Metrics Server must be running for CPU/Memory metrics.
Resource requests are required for percentage‑based scaling.

title: Persistent Volume Claim (PVC): Attach Storage to a Pod
objective: Create a PersistentVolume backed by hostPath and mount it into a pod, then write and read a file.
context: A stateful application needs a directory that persists across pod restarts on the local node.
tasks: Create a PersistentVolume named `host-pv` using `hostPath`.
Create a PersistentVolumeClaim `host-pvc` that binds to the PV.
Deploy a pod that mounts the PVC at `/data` and writes a file.
Delete the pod and recreate it to verify the data persists.
Cleanup the PVC, PV, and pod.
hints: A `hostPath` PV uses a directory on the node's filesystem. See PV docs: https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/storage/volumes/#hostpath
PVCs request storage; the PV must satisfy the claim's size and access mode.
Mount the PVC via a `volumeMount` in the pod spec.
Use `kubectl exec` to write and read files inside the container.
solution:
cat <<'EOF' > kcna-007-pv.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolume
metadata:
  name: host-pv
spec:
  capacity:
    storage: 1Gi
  accessModes:
  - ReadWriteOnce
  hostPath:
    path: /tmp/kcna-data
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: host-pvc
spec:
  accessModes:
  - ReadWriteOnce
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 1Gi
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: pvc-pod
spec:
  containers:
  - name: busybox
    image: busybox
    command: ["sh", "-c", "sleep 3600"]
    volumeMounts:
    - name: data-volume
      mountPath: /data
  volumes:
  - name: data-volume
    persistentVolumeClaim:
      claimName: host-pvc
EOF
kubectl apply -f kcna-007-pv.yaml
validation_commands: kubectl delete pod pvc-pod && kubectl run pvc-pod --image=busybox --restart=Never --command -- sh -c 'cat /data/greeting.txt'
key_concepts: PersistentVolumes provide cluster‑wide storage resources.
A PVC is a claim for storage that can be bound to a matching PV.
Data in a PV survives pod deletion, enabling stateful workloads.

title: RBAC: Grant Read‑Only Access to a Namespace
objective: Create a Role that allows read‑only access to all resources in a namespace and bind it to a user.
context: A junior developer needs to view resources in the `dev` namespace but must not be able to modify anything.
tasks: Create a namespace `dev`.
Create a Role `dev-reader` that grants `get`, `list`, and `watch` on all resource kinds.
Create a ServiceAccount `reader-sa` in the `dev` namespace.
Bind the Role to the ServiceAccount via a RoleBinding.
Verify the ServiceAccount can list pods but cannot create them.
Cleanup all created objects.
hints: Roles are namespace‑scoped; see RBAC docs: https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/access-authn-authz/rbac/#role-and-clusterrole
RoleBinding links a Role to a subject (user, group, or ServiceAccount).
Use `kubectl auth can-i` with the `--as` flag to test permissions for the ServiceAccount.
solution:
cat <<'EOF' > kcna-008-rbac.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: dev
---
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: Role
metadata:
  name: dev-reader
  namespace: dev
rules:
- apiGroups: [""]
  resources: ["*"]
  verbs: ["get","list","watch"]
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata:
  name: reader-sa
  namespace: dev
---
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: RoleBinding
metadata:
  name: dev-reader-binding
  namespace: dev
subjects:
- kind: ServiceAccount
  name: reader-sa
  namespace: dev
roleRef:
  kind: Role
  name: dev-reader
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
EOF
kubectl apply -f kcna-008-rbac.yaml
validation_commands: kubectl auth can-i list pods --as=system:serviceaccount:dev:reader-sa -n dev
kubectl auth can-i create pods --as=system:serviceaccount:dev:reader-sa -n dev
key_concepts: RBAC controls who can do what in the cluster.
Roles are scoped to a namespace; ClusterRoles apply cluster‑wide.
RoleBindings associate a Role with a user, group, or ServiceAccount.

title: Pod Disruption Budget (PDB): Maintain Availability During Upgrades
objective: Create a Deployment of three replicas and a PodDisruptionBudget that ensures at least two pods remain available during voluntary disruptions.
context: During a rolling upgrade of the node pool you must guarantee the service stays available.
tasks: Deploy a Deployment named `web-app` with 3 replicas of `nginx`.
Create a PodDisruptionBudget `web-pdb` with `minAvailable: 2`.
Simulate a node drain and verify that at most one pod is evicted.
Observe that the Deployment respects the PDB and maintains two running pods.
Cleanup resources.
hints: PDBs protect pods from voluntary disruptions like node drains. See PDB docs: https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/pods/disruptions/
`minAvailable` can be an absolute number or a percentage.
Use `kubectl drain <node>` to trigger evictions; the PDB will block excess evictions.
solution:
cat <<'EOF' > kcna-009-pdb.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: web-app
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: web
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: web
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nginx
        image: nginx:alpine
        ports:
        - containerPort: 80
---
apiVersion: policy/v1
kind: PodDisruptionBudget
metadata:
  name: web-pdb
spec:
  minAvailable: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: web
EOF
kubectl apply -f kcna-009-pdb.yaml
validation_commands: kubectl get nodes -o name | head -1 | xargs -I{} kubectl drain {} --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data --force
cleanup: kubectl delete -f kcna-009-pdb.yaml && kubectl uncordon $(kubectl get nodes -o name | head -1)
key_concepts: PDBs limit the number of pods that can be voluntarily evicted.
Useful for maintaining service availability during node maintenance or rolling updates.
`minAvailable` ensures a minimum number of ready pods; `maxUnavailable` works inversely.

title: Troubleshooting: Diagnose a CrashLoopBackOff Pod
objective: Deploy a pod with a misconfigured command that crashes, then use `kubectl describe` and logs to identify and fix the issue.
context: A newly created microservice fails to start due to a typo in the entrypoint command, causing a CrashLoopBackOff.
tasks: Create a pod `faulty-pod` that runs `nginx -g 'daemon off;'` but misspells the flag (e.g., `-g 'daemon off'`).
Observe the pod entering CrashLoopBackOff.
Use `kubectl describe pod` and `kubectl logs` to find the error.
Patch the pod spec to correct the command and verify it runs.
Cleanup the pod.
hints: `kubectl get pods` shows the status; `kubectl describe` reveals the last state and reason.
`kubectl logs` fetches the container’s stdout/stderr from the last attempt.
To fix, you can delete and recreate the pod with the corrected command or use `kubectl patch`.
solution:
cat <<'EOF' > kcna-010-faulty.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: faulty-pod
spec:
  containers:
  - name: nginx
    image: nginx:alpine
    command: ["nginx", "-g", "daemon off"] # missing trailing semicolon causes syntax error
EOF
kubectl apply -f kcna-010-faulty.yaml
validation_commands:
cat <<'EOF2' > kcna-010-fixed.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: fixed-pod
spec:
  containers:
  - name: nginx
    image: nginx:alpine
    command: ["nginx", "-g", "daemon off;"]
EOF
kubectl apply -f kcna-010-fixed.yaml
key_concepts: CrashLoopBackOff indicates a container repeatedly fails to start.
`kubectl describe` shows the last state and exit code.
`kubectl logs --previous` retrieves logs from the previous container instance.
Fixing the command or image resolves the loop.
